DOCUMENT:
Pricing Proposal: Weekend Rate Restructure
Harbourside Hotel, Revenue Management, April 2026

1. Proposal
From 1 June 2026 we propose to (a) raise the Best Available Rate (BAR) for Friday and Saturday nights from £145 to £165, and (b) introduce a two-night minimum for any stay that includes a Saturday night. Midweek rates are unchanged.

2. Context
Harbourside is a 112-room four-star hotel on the quay, with a leisure-led weekend business and a corporate-led midweek business. Our weekend BAR is £20 to £35 below the three comparable hotels in our competitive set, whose weekend rates currently range from £165 to £180. Weekend occupancy has recovered strongly since 2023 and we believe we are leaving money on the table.

Table 1. Weekend (Friday and Saturday) occupancy by month, 2025
Jan 62% | Feb 66% | Mar 74% | Apr 80% | May 85% | Jun 81%
Jul 89% | Aug 93% | Sep 88% | Oct 82% | Nov 72% | Dec 78%

Average weekend occupancy across 2025 was 79%. July and August are our strongest months, driven by the harbour festival and the school summer holidays, with September also benefiting from late-season visitors.

3. Evidence on price sensitivity
In the last week of June 2025 we raised the weekend BAR by £10, from £135 to the current £145. Weekend occupancy in July rose to 89%, from 81% in June. This tells us that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current levels; if anything, the higher rate appears to have reinforced our positioning as a quality option, and we expect the further increase to be absorbed in the same way.

This is consistent with feedback from our guest satisfaction surveys, where weekend guests rate "value for money" at 8.4 out of 10, the highest score among our competitive set.

4. Two-night minimum
Saturday nights are our most constrained inventory: we sold out on 31 Saturdays in 2025. Many of these guests stay only one night, leaving rooms empty on Friday or Sunday either side. A two-night minimum for stays including a Saturday will convert single-night Saturday stays into two-night stays and smooth occupancy across the weekend.

Our booking data show that weddings at Quayside Hall, the venue next door, account for around 38% of our Saturday-night room bookings. Wedding guests typically book as a block through the couple, arrive on the Saturday afternoon and check out on the Sunday morning.

5. Revenue impact
Across our 124 rooms, 104 weekend nights a year and average weekend occupancy of 79%, a £20 increase in BAR is worth about £204,000 a year in additional room revenue, before any gain from longer stays. We have assumed weekend occupancy is maintained at 2025 levels, which we consider prudent given the evidence above.

The two-night minimum should add further revenue through additional Friday and Sunday nights. We have not quantified this but expect it to be material, particularly in shoulder months.

6. Implementation and monitoring
The new rates will be loaded into the channel manager on 15 May for stays from 1 June, giving online travel agencies two weeks' notice. Corporate contracted rates and group rates already contracted will be honoured. We will review pick-up weekly against the same weeks in 2025 and report to the General Manager monthly. If weekend occupancy for any month falls more than five points below 2025, we will review the rate.

7. Recommendation
The evidence shows that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current rates and that we are priced well below our competitive set. We recommend approval of the £165 weekend BAR and the two-night Saturday minimum from 1 June 2026, delivering at least £204,000 of additional annual room revenue.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [inconsistency] at: "Across our 124 rooms, 104 weekend nights a year and average weekend occupancy of 79%" -- The hotel is described as a 112-room hotel in the Context section, but the revenue estimate uses 124 rooms. With 112 rooms the same calculation gives 112 x 104 x 0.79 x £20 = about £184,000, not £204,000.
2. [unsupported_causal] at: "This tells us that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current levels" -- The only evidence is that occupancy rose from June to July after a June rate rise, but the document itself says July and August are the strongest months because of the harbour festival and school holidays. The seasonal rise confounds the comparison; it cannot show demand is price-insensitive (let alone that the higher price helped).
3. [missing_consideration] at: "We have assumed weekend occupancy is maintained at 2025 levels, which we consider prudent given the evidence above." -- The document states that about 38% of Saturday-night bookings are wedding guests from the adjacent venue who stay only Saturday night. A two-night minimum would exclude or deter this group, but the revenue case assumes occupancy is maintained and never addresses the loss of these single-night Saturday bookings.

REVIEW:
# Review: Harbourside Weekend Rate Restructure

**Verdict:** A higher weekend rate may well be justified: you are priced below the competitive set, and the arithmetic leaves a fair margin for error (§4). But the proposal's main evidence doesn't show what it claims. The revenue figure uses the wrong room count and is a ceiling, not a floor. The two-night minimum directly conflicts with the wedding business described in the same section.

## What checks out

- The 2025 monthly occupancy figures average 79.2%, matching the stated 79%.
- The competitor gap is correct: £145 against £165–£180 is £20–£35 below.
- 104 weekend nights a year is correct (52 Fridays and 52 Saturdays).

## 1. The price-sensitivity "test" is the seasonal peak

The proposal treats July's rise from 81% to 89% as the response to the £10 increase. Its own Section 2 gives the explanation: July and August are the peak, "driven by the harbour festival and the school summer holidays." The data fit that reading:
- **It was already the peak.** A June-to-July rise happens every summer, so it would have happened whatever the rate.
- **The new rate barely touched July.** The increase came in the last week of June, so most July bookings were probably made at the old rate.
- **There is no year-on-year comparison.** Without July 2024, nobody can tell whether July 2025 was above or below what it would otherwise have been.

The 2025 rate change, as presented, is not evidence that guests are insensitive to price. The claim that it "reinforced our positioning" has no support at all.

**What would settle it:** compare weekend occupancy and booking pace before and after the June 2025 change against the same weeks in 2024. Alternatively, compare across the competitive set if benchmarking data are available.

## 2. The value-for-money score cuts the other way

A score of 8.4 was earned at £135–£145, while you were the cheapest hotel in the set. A high value score partly *reflects* the low price. It suggests guests are happy, not that they would stay happy at competitor prices. After the change you would be priced level with the cheapest competitor.

## 3. The revenue figure is overstated and is not a floor

**Wrong room count.** Section 2 says 112 rooms, but the calculation uses 124:
- 124 × 104 × 0.79 × £20 = **£203,800**
- 112 × 104 × 0.79 × £20 = **£184,000**

**Not every occupied room pays BAR.** The £20 rise applies only to rooms sold at the Best Available Rate. The calculation assumes every occupied weekend room pays it, but:
- Contracted corporate and group rates are honoured.
- Wedding blocks make up about 38% of Saturday bookings and are presumably sold at group rates.
- Rooms sold through online travel agents lose commission, often 15–20%.

The true figure depends on what share of weekend rooms sell at BAR, which the proposal doesn't give. It is likely well below £184,000.

**Two assumptions make the figure a ceiling, not a floor:**
- *Unchanged occupancy after a 14% rate rise.* That is the most favourable assumption, not a conservative one.
- *The two-night minimum only adds revenue.* It can lose Saturday nights from guests who want one night and go elsewhere. Its net effect could be negative.

## 4. The two-night minimum conflicts with the wedding business

Section 4 says wedding guests account for about 38% of Saturday bookings and stay exactly one night, Saturday to Sunday. A blanket two-night minimum on Saturday stays either:
- turns those guests away,
- forces them to pay for a night they won't use, which risks the relationship with Quayside Hall, or
- needs an exemption the proposal doesn't mention.

"Corporate and group commitments are protected" covers only bookings *already contracted*. It says nothing about weddings booked after 1 June.

A minimum stay also helps only on nights that would sell out anyway. In 2025 that was 31 Saturdays. On the other 21, it turns away one-night guests with no one to replace them. The usual practice is to apply minimum stays to specific high-demand dates, not as a standing rule.

## 5. A better case for the rate rise

The proposal doesn't need the July argument. At £165 against £145, weekend revenue holds up even if occupied room-nights fall by about 12%, since 145/165 ≈ 0.88. That means occupancy could fall from 79% to roughly 70% before the rise loses room revenue. Lost food, drink and other spend would lower that tolerance somewhat.

The monitoring trigger, a fall of more than five points below 2025, sits well inside that margin, so it is reasonably cautious. Two improvements:
- Track revenue per available room and booking pace, not occupancy alone.
- Act on weekly pick-up data rather than waiting for month-end results.

## Summary of the author's claims

| Claim | Assessment |
|---|---|
| Built on our own trading history | The key data point is the seasonal peak, not a price test |
| June 2025 rise shows guests aren't price sensitive | Not supported |
| Value score of 8.4 supports the rise | Reflects the current low price; doesn't show tolerance of a higher one |
| £20–£35 below competitors | Correct |
| £204,000 is a floor | Wrong room count (£184k with 112), and it assumes every room pays BAR. It is a ceiling. |
| No value placed on extra Friday and Sunday nights | True, but the minimum stay can also lose Saturdays; the net effect is unknown |
| Corporate and group commitments protected | Only contracts already in place; future weddings are exposed |
| Monitoring will catch a dip | Broadly fine; better on revenue per room and weekly pace |
| Well-evidenced, low-risk | The rate rise is plausible but under-evidenced; the minimum stay as designed is not low-risk |

## Suggested revisions

1. Correct the room count, and base revenue on BAR-sold rooms net of commission.
2. Replace the July argument with a year-on-year comparison and the break-even analysis in §5.
3. Apply the minimum stay only to high-demand dates, with wedding blocks explicitly exempt or agreed with Quayside Hall.
4. Present the revenue figure as a range, with an estimate of how many guests the rate rise and minimum stay would lose.
